texts.error.godot_older: This game was made with Godot %1.%2.%3: open it with the Godot 4.%4 core, which also runs games of older Godot 4 versions.
texts.error.godot_other: This game was made with Godot %1.%2.%3: open it with the Godot 4.%4 core (this one runs Godot 4.%5 games).
texts.error.godot_too_new: This game was made with Godot %1.%2.%3, newer than every Godot core (the newest runs Godot 4.%4 games).

texts.setting.drawingcode.about: Which of the CPU's instructions the code that draws the pictures may use. AVX2 (the default): also those of most PCs made since 2013, which draw faster; on a computer without them the baseline is used, and the pictures may then differ from another computer's by a shade. Baseline: only those every 64-bit PC has, so a movie gives the same pictures on any computer. The game itself plays the same either way.
texts.setting.drawingsize.about: How big a picture the game draws, against the size it asks for. Godot draws every pixel on the CPU here, so a game drawn at 50% has a quarter of the pixels and runs up to about four times faster. The picture is shown at the same size, softer. The game is told its window is that size: one that stretches its picture to its window (most) draws smaller, one that draws at a fixed size of its own is not made faster. It is part of the machine, so a movie needs the same value.
texts.setting.framerate.about: How many frames make a second of the game's time. Godot runs one step of the game per frame and tells the game that 1/rate of a second went by, as if its monitor refreshed at this rate. 60 is what most games are made for. It is part of the machine, so a movie needs the same value.
texts.setting.starttime.about: The date and time the game reads (Time.get_unix_time_from_system and the date functions) when it starts, in seconds since 1970 (Unix time), in UTC; it then runs with the frames. The default is the first of January 2000. This is a setting, and not your computer's clock, so that a movie plays back the same on any day. It is part of the machine, so a movie needs the same value.
texts.setting.verbose.about: 'true' starts Godot with --verbose, so that its log (Tools > Export Core Log, or the console) says what it loads and draws. It changes nothing in the game.
texts.slot.files.help: Files the game opens from the folder its executable is in, under the names it asks for: a second .pck it loads (downloadable content, a mod), or data it reads beside itself. A game that loads nothing else needs nothing here.
texts.slot.pack.help: The game's .pck file, which an exported Godot game keeps beside its executable (Game.exe and Game.pck). A game exported as a single file has the .pck inside its executable: then give the executable (.exe or .x86_64) instead.
texts.slot.savedata.help: What the game keeps in user:// (its saves and settings), as Emulator > Export Save Data wrote it: each file under its own name, or the .zip the export makes of several. They are put in user:// before the game starts, so the game finds them as its own. A file of the export that was in a folder of user:// goes back in that folder only from the .zip.
